result:
The proposed answer of 0 is not justified, so I reject it.

The reduction is sound. Inside a weak Sidon set, a subset is Sidon exactly when it has no three-term progression. Each middle index supports at most one progression, so there are at most $n-2$ progressions. The counting then gives $h(A) \ge c\,n^{2/3}$ for every weak Sidon set $A$ of size $n$.

The problem is the final step. A lower bound $g(n) = \Omega(n^{2/3})$ gives only $g(n)/n \ge c\,n^{-1/3}$, which says nothing about whether $g(n)/n$ tends to 0. Showing the limit is 0 requires an upper bound $g(n) = o(n)$, meaning explicit weak Sidon sets whose largest Sidon subsets are small. The solution never constructs such sets. Its argument therefore does not establish the limit, and I have not verified independently whether the true limit is 0.

VERDICT: REJECT
CONFIDENCE: 4
